message:
QUESTION: Which of the three tariffs (Fixed, Variable or Time-of-use) will give the household the lowest total energy bill over the next 12 months, and by how much? DATA: A household is choosing an energy tariff for the next 12 months (365 days). It is currently on the Variable tariff and can switch freely: none of the tariffs below has an exit fee. Last 12 months' usage: electricity 3,100 kWh, gas 12,000 kWh. About 15% of the household's current electricity use falls in the off-peak window (dishwasher and washing machine on timers). The household takes delivery of an electric car next week. It expects to need about 2,400 kWh a year of home charging, all of which it will schedule in the off-peak window. Gas use is not expected to change. | Tariff | Electricity unit rate | Electricity standing charge | Gas unit rate | Gas standing charge | | Fixed (F) | 24.5p/kWh | 55p/day | 6.2p/kWh | 30p/day | | Variable (V) | 22.0p/kWh | 60p/day | 6.0p/kWh | 31p/day | | Time-of-use (E) | 30.0p/kWh peak; 8.0p/kWh off-peak (00:30-05:30) | 50p/day | 6.0p/kWh | 31p/day | Rates on V can change at the supplier's discretion with 30 days' notice; the supplier has announced no change. F and E are fixed for 12 months. Ignore VAT (rates already include it). Here is your current analysis: # Energy Tariff Comparison for the Next 12 Months ## Answer **Time-of-use (E) gives the lowest bill: £2,035.35 for the year.** - That is **£226.80 less than staying on Variable (V)**, which costs £2,262.15. V is the next-cheapest option. - It is **£366.40 less than Fixed (F)**, which costs £2,401.75. The car arrives next week, so it will charge for about 51 weeks of the 52. That trims the realistic saving against V to **about £220**. The ranking does not change. ## Usage for the next 12 months | | Peak | Off-peak | Total | |---|---|---|---| | Existing use (3,100 kWh, 15% off-peak) | 2,635 | 465 | 3,100 | | Car charging (all off-peak) | 0 | 2,400 | 2,400 | | **Total electricity** | **2,635** | **2,865** | **5,500** | | Gas (unchanged) | | | 12,000 | ## Costs (365 days) | | Fixed (F) | Variable (V) | Time-of-use (E) | |---|---|---|---| | Electricity units | 5,500 × 24.5p = £1,347.50 | 5,500 × 22.0p = £1,210.00 | 2,635 × 30p = £790.50
2,865 × 8p = £229.20 | | Electricity standing charge | 55p × 365 = £200.75 | 60p × 365 = £219.00 | 50p × 365 = £182.50 | | **Electricity total** | **£1,548.25** | **£1,429.00** | **£1,202.20** | | Gas units | 12,000 × 6.2p = £744.00 | 12,000 × 6.0p = £720.00 | 12,000 × 6.0p = £720.00 | | Gas standing charge | 30p × 365 = £109.50 | 31p × 365 = £113.15 | 31p × 365 = £113.15 | | **Gas total** | **£853.50** | **£833.15** | **£833.15** | | **Annual total** | **£2,401.75** | **£2,262.15** | **£2,035.35** | | **Extra cost compared with E** | **+£366.40** | **+£226.80** | n/a | ## Why E wins - **Gas costs the same on V and E**, so all of E's advantage comes from electricity. - **The car makes the difference.** On last year's usage alone, E would cost **£109.20 more** than V (£1,010.20 against £901.00). Most existing use is at peak, where E charges 30p against V's 22p. - **Off-peak charging is much cheaper on E.** Each kWh charged off-peak costs 8p on E against 22p on V, a saving of 14p. Over 2,400 kWh that is £336. That covers the £109.20 penalty and leaves £226.80. - **F is dearer than V at this household's usage.** - F's unit rates are higher for both fuels, which adds £161.50. - F's standing charges are lower for both fuels (5p and 1p a day), which saves £21.90. - Net, F costs £139.60 more. - F would only beat V for a household using very little energy. ## How robust is the result? | Risk | E stays cheapest as long as… | Likelihood of failure | |---|---|---| | Less car charging than expected | Off-peak car charging is at least **780 kWh** (£109.20 ÷ 14p). | Low. That is about a third of the estimate. | | Some charging happens at peak | No more than about **1,030 kWh** (about 43%) of charging is at peak. Each kWh moved to peak adds 22p to E's bill. | Low, if charging is scheduled. | | V's electricity rate is cut | V's rate stays above about **17.9p** for the whole year. With 30 days' notice, a cut could apply for at most about 11 months, so V would need to fall to about **17.5p**. | Low. No change has been announced. A rise in V's rates only widens E's lead. | **F only becomes the best choice if two things go wrong at once:** - More than about 1,665 kWh (about 70%) of charging lands at peak, so F beats E. - V's rates rise enough to make V dearer than F. At this usage, V's electricity rate would need to rise by about 2.5p for the full year, or about 2.8p if the rise starts after the notice period. **None of these risks locks the household in.** No tariff has exit fees, so the household can switch at no cost if any of these risks materialises. **There is upside too.** Each extra kWh of existing use moved into the off-peak window, for example the tumble dryer, saves a further 22p on E. **The off-peak window is long enough.** 2,400 kWh a year averages about 6.6 kWh a night. - A 7 kW charger delivers that in about an hour. - A 3-pin plug at about 2.3 kW delivers about 11.5 kWh in the 5-hour window. That covers the average night, but a very depleted battery may need more than one night. ## Recommendation **Switch to Time-of-use (E).** It saves about £220 over the year against staying on V and about £360 against F. It also fixes prices for 12 months. To get the saving, the household should: 1. **Check the meter.** E needs a smart meter that records peak and off-peak use separately. 2. **Confirm the off-peak hours with the supplier.** Some meters keep the window in GMT, which means 01:30–06:30 during British Summer Time. Set the car and appliance timers to match. 3. **Set the car to charge only in the off-peak window.** Also check that the car's app does not top up or pre-heat the car at peak. Keep the dishwasher and washing machine timers as they are. 4. **Check peak use on the first couple of bills.** - Compare each month's peak use with the same month last year, not with the annual average. Winter use is naturally higher. - If peak use is running **more than about 40 kWh a month** above last year, roughly 20% of charging is landing at peak. At that point, fix the scheduling. - At about **85 kWh a month** above last year, E's saving over V is gone. If the scheduling cannot be fixed, switch back to V. --- ### What I changed in this review - **Re-verified every figure.** The totals, the differences, the 780, 1,030 and 1,665 kWh thresholds, the 17.9p and 17.5p thresholds, and the roughly £220 part-year saving are all correct. - **Fixed the bill-check trigger.** The old draft said 85 kWh a month above baseline meant "roughly 40%" of charging was at peak. In fact 85 kWh a month is about 43%, which is the break-even point where the saving has already disappeared. That made it a poor early warning. There is now a separate early-warning level (about 40 kWh a month) and a break-even level. - **Fixed the baseline for that check.** The old draft compared each month with the flat 220 kWh annual average. Winter peak use would routinely exceed that and trigger false alarms. The comparison is now with the same month last year. - **Quantified the V rise needed for F to win** (about 2.5–2.8p), which the old draft left vague. - **Added the upside** of shifting more existing appliance use into the off-peak window. - **Labelled the V-cut risk as electricity only.** Gas rates are identical on V and E, so a gas change would affect both comparisons differently and is outside this threshold. Review it critically and produce an improved version.
